sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Channels are excellent for communicating data between goroutines, but they are the wrong tool when multiple goroutines need to read and write shared mutable state — caches, counters, registries, lazy-initialized singletons. The sync package provides the low-level primitives for these cases. Interviewers test sync knowledge to verify that candidates understand Go's memory model, can recognize data races, and know when not to reach for channels. Misusing sync (copying a mutex, not calling Done, forgetting to unlock) are real bugs found in production Go codebases.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: `sync.Mutex` grants exclusive access — one goroutine holds the lock; all others block. `sync.RWMutex` is an optimization for read-heavy workloads: any number of goroutines can hold a read lock simultaneously, but a write lock is exclusive. `sync.WaitGroup` is a countdown latch — call `Add(n)` before launching goroutines, `Done()` inside each goroutine, and `Wait()` to block until the count reaches zero. `sync.Once` guarantees a function runs exactly once regardless of how many goroutines call it — canonical for lazy singleton initialization. `sync.Pool` is a free-list for temporarily reusing objects to reduce GC pressure.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **sync.Mutex / RWMutex**: always `defer mu.Unlock()` immediately after `mu.Lock()` to ensure unlock even on panic; RLock/RUnlock for reads, Lock/Unlock for writes.
- **sync.WaitGroup**: `Add` must be called before the goroutine is launched (not inside it) to avoid a race between Add and Wait.
- **sync.Once**: `once.Do(f)` — f runs exactly once; subsequent calls are no-ops; used for initializing global state, DB connections, config.
- **sync.Pool**: items in a Pool may be reclaimed by the GC at any time; always check for nil on Get; used by fmt, encoding/json to reuse buffers.
- **sync.Map**: concurrent map optimized for high read, low write or disjoint key sets; not a general replacement for `map` + mutex.
- **sync/atomic**: lock-free operations on integers and pointers; `atomic.AddInt64`, `atomic.LoadInt64`, `atomic.CompareAndSwapInt64` — the building block of higher-level primitives.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **Copy lock pitfall**: a `sync.Mutex` must never be copied after first use — embedding it in a struct that is passed by value creates two independent mutexes. Use pointer receivers and pass structs by pointer.
- **WaitGroup.Add inside goroutine**: if you call `wg.Add(1)` inside the goroutine body, `wg.Wait()` may return before the goroutine has even registered — always Add before `go`.
- **Mutex vs channel decision**: channels for ownership transfer and signalling; mutex for protecting shared state. When data doesn't need to move between goroutines, a mutex is simpler.
- **Deadlock with deferred unlock**: calling an RLock inside a function that already holds a write lock deadlocks — Go's mutexes are not reentrant.
- **go vet and race detector**: `go test -race` catches data races; `go vet` catches copied mutexes and mismatched Lock/Unlock.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "When I need shared mutable state accessed by multiple goroutines — say a cache or a registry — I reach for sync.RWMutex rather than channels, because there's no data transfer, just shared access that needs coordination. I always defer Unlock immediately after Lock so the mutex is released even if the function panics. For one-time initialization like a singleton DB connection, sync.Once is my go-to because it's guaranteed to run exactly once with no double-check locking needed. One subtle issue I always watch for is copying a mutex — structs that embed a Mutex must always be passed by pointer, never by value, otherwise you silently create two independent locks protecting different copies of the same data."
